findings.what: No screen ever shows the two rules, 30 − 0.04q² for the pump and 10 + 0.06q² for the pipe with q in L/s, so screen 2's '30 − 4 = 26 m' and '10 + 6 = 16 m' and screen 1's 14.1 L/s at 22.0 m come from nowhere; give screen 1 both rules and the one-line solve 0.1q² = 20, q² = 200 (about 20 words; the screen has no live line, so 62 + 20 stays under 90).

'A pump gives its most head at no flow' is stated for every pump, and screen 11's positive displacement pump breaks it; say 'A centrifugal pump' and call this one an example pump, since no screen says the curves are sketches.

'NPSH required is the least absolute pressure the pump needs there' puts it at the impeller's eye, but it is set at the pump's suction (inlet), and its job is to cover the further drop into the eye; say 'at its inlet' and add that the pressure falls further on the way into the eye, which also explains why the eye is the low point.

The brief promised mixed puzzles over the whole course, but no puzzle reaches back before lesson 7, and screen 12 just repeats the answer screen 11 gave a moment earlier; swap screen 12 for one that does, such as the shut-valve case: 3.0 kW into 5 kg of trapped seawater warms it about 0.16 °C a second (Q = mcΔT, lesson 1), and warmer water boils more easily, so the pump nears cavitation.

'The valve ×4 dot shows full speed, throttled instead' talks in the key's labels; say it plainly, for example 'The faint dot is the same pump at full speed, throttled instead: less flow for more power.'

When the level is dragged, both tanks drop together, and no word says why (the lift is held at 10 m so only the suction changes); add a short clause, trimming elsewhere, because the text plus the longest live line is already about 88 of 90 words.

No screen says why cavitation matters (noise, a pitted impeller), and none ties boiling at low pressure to water boiling at 100 °C at normal pressure; one short sentence each would complete the why, within the same word budget.

It says where the efficiency hump peaks, near 14 L/s at about 71%, but never that a pump is chosen to run near that peak (a brief promise); the open-valve point at 14.1 L/s sits right on it, so one sentence makes the point.
'it reads the pump's head' is loose: the outlet gauge reads the suction pressure plus what the pump adds, so say it rises with the pump's head.

findings.where: Pump scene, screens 1, 3 and 4 (360 light and dark pictures)
findings.what: At level +2 m the dashed suction-level line runs through the impeller and along the motor's top edge, which clutters the pump; stop it short of the pump or draw it behind the pump.

There are seven footnote markers ([^3] and [^4] twice each, and [^6] on 'bends up more steeply', which is not a rule he would look up); keep about three, for the operating point, NPSH and the shut-valve power.

'It rattles like gravel and can pit the impeller' and 'That is why it is fitted with a relief valve' have no quote in sources[] or research-notes.md (the fact-check reply marked both 'textbooks add'); they are standard knowledge, but each needs a source or should stay plainly general.

The brief's marine example, fire pumps and pumping systems, never appears; screen 13's cooling pump is the only marine example, and naming a fire or bilge main once on screen 7 or 13 would anchor it at sea.
